speechtext:
No, it would not, but
the position is precisely the same. Under the disputes act, if there is a difference of opinion between the railway company and its employees, the employees appoint their representative to act as arbitrator. The company appoints another and the chairman is nominated either by the two or by the Minister of Labour, and thus the board of arbitration is constituted. In the present instance there

C.N.R.-CR.R. Bill
may be a dispute between the two railway companies as to wihat is to be done in a particular case-whether they will take off a through train of the Canadian Pacific and allow the Canadian National to do all the business, or vice versa. If an agreement cannot be reached, the matter will go to arbitration. My hon. friend's suggestion is that it be referred to a board made up entirely of nominees of the owners of one of the railways, and that the other railway shall not have any representation on the board at all.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: That is exactly what it means. The Board of Railway Commissioners is appointed by the government of Canada, parliament acting through the government, and it is suggested that the board shall be the sole arbitrator. Neither of the companies may be represented on it at all. On the other hand, the arbitral tribunal is just what it means, a board of arbitration to decide a dispute between the two railway companies, and one company has the same right to be represented as the other. Counsel for each railway may appear before that tribunal. My hon. friend says that it is counsel for both railways sitting in with the judge, but it is the arbitrator from each company sitting in with the chairman of the arbitral tribunal.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
There is this important difference so far as industrial disputes are concerned, that neither of the parties is bound to accept the decision of the board. Under this legislation it is not merely a matter of taking off a train or two, or anything of that sort, because if the hon. gentleman will look at the bill he will see that power is given with regard to the joint use of terminals, the running rights of one line over the other, the joint use of tracks, control and prohibition in respect of construction of new lines, joint use of facilities, the abandonment of lines, services and facilities, the pooling of any part or parts of freight or passenger traffic, and all things necessary and incidental thereto. These three gentlemen are to sit in private. I agree with the minister when he says that perhaps they could arrive at a better arrangement to their own way of thinking than they could sitting in open court, but are we going to provide that three men may sit down in private without the public knowing what they are doing or why they are doing it and decide upon the slaughtering of branch and main lines, the giving of running rights to one road
over the other, and the throwing of thousands of railroad men out of work? This is one thing above all others which should be decided out in the open so that the people interested might appear before the board.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest that because of the comprehensive powers granted to the tribunal, one of the parties to the arbitration should not be represented on the board?

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: No.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: That is his argument. There is no doubt that comprehensive powers are being given to these tribunals and my hon. friend is arguing that because of these comprehensive powers, one of the parties to the dispute should be represented on the board while the other is not.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member for East Algoma fully understands what I said. I have no objection to the two railroad companies being represented but I do contend that what is done by this board should be done in public and not in private. I would be quite satisfied to go right down stream with my hon. friend if he would get the government which he is supporting to follow the same procedure as that followed under the Industrial Disputes Act.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: I am not talking about whether the board will sit in private or public, I am referring to the amendment which provides that the Board of Railway Commissioners shall be the arbitral tribunal. This board is appointed by the owners of the Canadian National Railways and the amendment provides that they shall be the arbitral tribunal which may decide that the Canadian Pacific shall surrender a terminal to the Canadian National, that it shall abandon a line or other such matters. The Canadian Pacific would have no representative upon this tribunal. As the tribunal is now set up it is a board of arbitration purely and simply. Whether the dispute is great or small, each party will be represented. It is an entirely different matter to discuss how these arbitral tribunals shall carry out their work; I am referring now to the amendment which provides that the owners of the Canadian National Railways will appoint the arbitrators while the Canadian Pacific cannot make any appointment.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
The bill provides that a representative of both companies shall be a member of the tribunal, but it also provides
C.N.R.-CP.R. Bill

that the chairman of that tribunal, who is to be the chairman of the railway commission, must be satisfied with all decisions. In reality, he is the sole arbitrator.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: If the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is objecting to these tribunals simply because they may sit in private, his objection cannot stand. It is expressly provided in the Railway Act that the Board of Railway Commissioners may sit in private if they choose to do so. If the procedure followed by the Board of Railway Commissioners is to be adopted in the consideration of these matters, the sittings could be held in private.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: But the Board of Railway Commissioners or any other board has never had to deal with a bill like this. My point is that when the Board of Railway Commissioners or a tribunal is given powers such as those contained in this bill, their sittings should be held in the open.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: Then my hon. friend does not agree with the hon. member who has moved the amendment. The mover of the amendment asks that these matters be carried to the Board of Railway Commissioners. If that is done, the sittings could be held in private.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: We will have other amendments to offer.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
The hon. member for South Toronto and the hon. member for East Algoma have suggested important reasons why this amendment should not carry, but there are other reasons also why these matters could not be left to the Board of Railway Commissioners. I would refer the committee to clause 19 of the bill, which reads:
If, in the opinion of the presiding officer of any tribunal, any application made to him raises matters of substantial concern to the public or a section of the public, he may direct that notice of the sittings of the tribunal shall be given either by advertisement in one or more newspapers, or otherwise as he may consider expedient.
He may permit the public to be represented at the meetings. Therefore, it is provided by the bill that the public can get into these meetings.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: What provision is made to let the public know that the arbitral tribunal is going to deal with a certain matter?

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
If, in the opinion of the presiding officer of any tribunal, the matter to be considered affects a certain section of 
the public or the public as a whole, it would be his duty to notify the public either by advertisements in the public press, by personal letters or otherwise. He would also inform the attorney general of the province to which the matter under consideration referred. There are one or two other points which I think make the present arrangement more acceptable than having the Board of Railway Commissioners constitute the tribunal. The purpose of parts II and III of this bill is to bring about greater cooperation between the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways. As the bill distinctly states, it is to effect economies and provide more remunerative operation. That being the case, it seems to me to be much more reasonable to have a representative of each company upon the tribunal than to have the Board of Railway Commissioners constitute such tribunal. To a large extent this board has been dealing with questions such as freight rates and other similar matters.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
Would not the other
members of the railway commission become just as competent as the chairman to deal with these matters?

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
Possibly they would over
a period of time. It must be understood that the two railroads would not appoint the same representative to sit on all tribunals. They would appoint a representative who was familiar with the particular branch of the service with which the particular tribunal was to deal. A tribunal might be appointed to deal with the pooling or cooperation of telegraph lines or express services, and the railroads would appoint representatives who were familiar with telegraphic operation or express services, as the case may be. That is a very important and useful provision which could be worked out under this method of having a tribunal.
Another point is that the arbitral tribunal as set up by this bill may not have to give a decision at all. Being set up as it is in a more or less informal manner, I mean so far as its members are concerned, the chairman being the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners and the other two members being representatives of the two railways, and being able to sit down, as I suggested a little while ago, at a round table conference to discuss a matter, it is very likely, as the object of the two railways is to bring about greater cooperation and more economy, there will be a greater possibility of their coming to an agreement without any

C.N.R.-CR.R. Bill
formal judgment being given. That is really the whole object of part II and, indeed, of the bill so far as parts II and III are concerned, namely, to bring about greater cooperation and in that way save both companies from the pressure of competition, duplication and the consequent unnecessary expense. Having listened to the observations of hon. gentlemen opposite and two hon. gentlemen on this side who, besides myself, have taken part in the discussion, I should think the arguments are all for leaving in the bill the arbitral tribunal just as it is at present.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
Has the minister considered
the position in which this will put the chairman of the railway commission supposing a dispute should arise in which five commissioners decide it one way and the chairman decides it the other? The chairman would be overruled by the five others. He could then induce one of the railway companies to ask for a tribunal. He would be the sole arbiter on that and in that way he could defeat the purpose of the entire railway commission.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
I do not quite get my
hon. friend's point.	Is he referring to a
tribunal that has five men on it?

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
I understand the railway
commission has six members. Suppose a matter is referred to it; five of the members decide one way, and the chairman decides the other. Thp decision of the five would prevail. Then the chairman, not satisfied with that decision, could request one of the railway companies to ask for a tribunal. The matter would be referred to a tribunal of which he would be the sole arbiter and in that way he could defeat the entire purpose of the railway commission; he could overrule the five.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
Of course my hon. friend
is putting up a theoretical case which I do not think is likely to occur. As a matter of fact, generally speaking and without reflecting in any way upon the members of the railway .commission as it exists at present or as it was in the past, the chairman has been the outstanding member. I say that without any disrespect towards any other member of the commission. I do not think the case suggested by my hon. friend is likely to occur.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: It could occur.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
I do not suppose any
legislation can prevent some remote possibility from occurring. No legislation that is set up provides for every remote possibility. But I do not think the surmised case of the
hon. gentleman is likely to arise in practical railway questions.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: On other boards it frequently happens that one member will appose all the others, and I do not see why this might not occur on the railway commission.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
Another point that might
be put forward is that this would amount almost to a conspiracy. Supposing the board had given a decision and the chairman did not like the judgment the majority had given *against him. He would be conspiring with the two railway companies to defeat that.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: Not necessarily. The railway company that was not satisfied with the decision could ask for an arbitral tribunal.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: Then be would be conspiring with the one railway company to defeat the other.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: We have been considering what would take place if a tribunal were established, how one railway might get into difficulty with another, thereby bringing about the establishment of a tribunal and subsequently a solution of the matter that might not be satisfactory to some parts of Canada. What about the situation that might arise supposing the two railways deliberately never disagreed? There would then be no tribunal and a policy of inaction adopted from year to year. The roads would take the line of least resistance. In such a case, what would be the situation of parts of the country that would be seriously affected *by not having the necessary transportation facilities? I am afraid they would be in a bad way.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
In the past the railways
took the line of least resistance and they did not cooperate. I say quite frankly that when this government came into power, one of the first matters pointed out to the heads of both railway companies by the Prime Minister and myself was the need of greater cooperation. It is obvious to every hon. member and, indeed, to every citizen who cares to look about him, that there were great opportunities for cooperation in regard to a number of trains, for instance, those running between here and Montreal, Montreal and Toronto, and in other parts of the country. There were great opportunities for cooperation in ticket offices, for instance, those on Sparks street. We pointed out to the railway companies that there were these opportunities of cooperating and thereby saving money.
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

To-day, in view of the fact that this legislation is pending and that it carried practically unanimously in the other house, the railways are making an effort to cooperate to a greater extent than they ever did in the past. I do not think either railway would take the position suggested by the hon. gentleman, that is, merely to stand pat, or the management of the road would not be doing their duty towards it, because it is certainly the duty of both railways under present circumstances to endeavour to cooperate and to bring about more economical operation than has been the case for some years.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: I believe the two roads should cooperate as far as possible, but supposing they are opposed, as I believe they are, to this tribunal, the purpose of setting up the tribunal might be nullified by the failure of the railways to avail themselves of its services and the result that the public interest in the matter of transportation and other facilities would suffer. Where would the country be in a situation of this kind? I am afraid the transportation facilities of different areas of Canada would seriously suffer.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: The hon. member is out of order in discussing that. It comes under part III; it does not come under this clause.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: Well, I am putting it under.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: I have one other word to say. The minister suggests that this tribunal is going to be simply a round table conference. Under part II of the bill, the two railway companies are surely going to get together and have their round table conference before a matter comes to a dispute. When it comes to a dispute, it is time then to have some independent body to decide the question at issue. Such a dispute will be one in which the Canadian people are vitally interested and we should have a board in which the people have learned to have confidence and on which are men who are trained in the duties that this tribunal will have to undertake.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
Following that up and emphasizing what has been said with respect to the possibility of conflict between the Board of Railway Commissioners and the tribunal, let me put this case to the minister for the purpose of finding out just what this bill means and seeing if we are not in effect wiping out entirely the jurisdiction of the railway commission, at least with regard to the abandonment of lines. Assume, for instance, that the Canadian National Railway 
wants to abandon a line without reference to the Canadian Pacific. After this legislation is passed this matter will be under the jurisdiction of the board of trustees. It is said that those trustees cannot exercise the power to abandon the line without the recommendation of the Board of Railway Commissioners and the approval of the governor in council. That is to say, if they want to operate on their own, they must, as I understand the-minister, operate under section 23.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: May I make that clear? Only so far as the Canadian National is concerned. That does not affect the Canadian Northern or the Grand Trunk Pacific.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
I am talking about the
Canadian National. It has to have the recommendation of the railway board and the approval of the governor in council. Supposing the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National are in conflict in some particular area; they have possibly a duplicate service. The Canadian Pacific takes the initiative and asks the Canadian National to agree to abandon its line in order that the Canadian Pacific may operate. The Canadian National fails to agree. A dispute arises and the tribunal is formed. The tribunal orders the Canadian National to agree and therefore to abandon its line. What I want to be clear on is whether under such circumstances the Board of Railway Commissioners have power to keep the Canadian National from abandoning that line, or whether the tribunal, representing simply the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners and the two representatives- or one representative it may be-of the railway companies, has power not only to authorize but to require the Canadian National to do what section 23 says it cannot do without the approval of the governor in council and the recommendation of the Board of Railway Commissioners. May I refer to section 23 of this bill, which provides that:
Where the execution of an order, or the carrying out of a decision of a tribunal, involves the doing of any act which by any statute requires, but for the provisions of this act, Lie leave, sanction, assent or approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners, or where in the opinion of the presiding officer the public interests involved are of sufficient importance to warrant it, no order made by a tribunal shall be operative without the concurrence of the presiding officer and his formal written assent.
Section 24 reads:
In the event of any conflict between an order of the Board of Railway Commissioners and that of any tribunal, the order or decision of the tribunal shall prevail.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
That it seems to me, makes it perfectly clear that the Canadian Pacific Railway, on a definite and-shall I say?-hostile application involving a dispute and the convening of the tribunal, can succeed in having the Canadian National forced to override the provisions of section 23 and abandon a line which otherwise it could not do without the approval of the governor in council and the board.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend
has interpreted it correctly, but that is just as true of the Canadian National forcing the Canadian Pacific to do the same thing.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
No, the Canadian Pacific
*does not require the approval of the governor in council nor of the board.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
That is true, but so far
as the abandonment of a line is concerned the tribunal has the same power to force the Canadian Pacific as to force the Canadian National to abandon. My hon. friend will agree to that.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: Section 23 of the Canadian National Railways Act really refers only to the Grand Trunk Railway. It is true that that may be wiped out by the arbitral tribunal under this act, but as I said, that section applies only to the Grand Trunk. At the present time the Canadian Northern or the drand Trunk Pacific and their subsidiaries could abandon their lines without the consent of the Board of Railway Commissioners just as the Canadian Pacific could; but the Grand Trunk could not, because the Grand Trunk is the railway constituting the Canadian National Railway Company.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: I think the minister is absolutely right when he states that the [DOT]Canadian Pacific has the right under existing law to abandon part of its permanent line; but on the other hand, is it not true that the community that would be affected by the abandonment of that line have a perfect Tight to appeal to the Board of Railway Commissioners, and if a judgment is given by the *board, that judgment rules?

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
My hon. friend is partly
right, to this extent, that if the Canadian Pacific had received a subsidy, for instance, from this government, and in consequence had agreed to carry on a particular service, it could not abandon that service, or if it had made an agreement with or received assistance from a local community and had agreed to carry on a certain service, it could not abandon that service because that would be an agreement as binding as any other
agreement. But apart from an agreement of that kind, binding the company because of some subsidy given by this government or some other government, the Canadian Pacific I am informed, and I think it is absolutely correct, could discontinue a service.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: I think the minister is correct. But the community affected by the abandonment of that service or line has the right to appeal to the Board of Railway Commissioners, and if judgment is given by the board it applies to the Canadian Pacific just the same as to everybody else.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: That is true. The public might appeal to the Board of Railway Commissioners, but the Canadian Pacific can abandon a line unless it is tied by an agreement, contract, or subsidy to carry on that service, and it can abandon it without appealing to the board at all.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: My hon. friend says that section 23 applies only to the Canadian Northern.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: The Grand Trunk, I said.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
Just on what does the
minister base that statement? As I understand section 19 of the Canadian National Railways Act, it permits the putting of any railway under the operation and management of the Canadian National Railways.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: I do not like to attempt to express the legal reasons, but the actual fact is that the only railway in the Canadian National Railways is the Grand Trunk railway and the branch lines which have been built in recent years have also been put under the Canadian National Railways Act.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: The Canadian Northern was under the Canadian National.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: For operation. The Canadian government railways are under the control of the government. That is the difference. But the Grand Trunk is the only one under the Canadian National Railways Act.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: Surely the abandonment of lines is operation.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: It is the very opposite to operation.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
Does not abandonment
come within the term "operation"?

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: I do not quite follow the question.	.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
The governor in council has power to vest in the Canadian National Railway Company the management and operation of any road, and the governor in council
39S4
C.N.R.-CR.R. Bill

has done that in the case of the Canadian government railways, the Canadian Northern, and the Grand Trunk Pacific; and in the case of the Grand Trunk the Canadian National actually owns the stock. Under section 23 of the Canadian National Railways Act, with the approval of the governor in council, the company may abandon the operation of any lines or parts of lines. I submit that that applies directly to the lines which the company is empowered to operate, and it applies not only to the Grand Trunk but to the Canadian government railways and other roads as well. The very words of the section are "may abandon the operation of any lines or parts of lines." In a previous section the governor in council has vested in the Canadian National Railway Company the operation of all these different railways. This means only that it may cease to operate them.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: That is not my information. Section 23 applies to the Grand Trunk, and it would apply also to the branch lines that were built under the Canadian National Railways Act.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: I cannot believe that the abandonment of operation of a Canadian government railway line is to be permitted without the approval of the governor in council.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: That is a different matter.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATION AL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
This is the section which requires the approval of the governor in council before the operation of any line can be abandoned. My hon. friend says that the Canadian government railways are not within that section. There must be something wrong with that.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
